---
title: "Quiz: evaluation against ground truth"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. TP, FP, FN and TN count the pixels of a predicted mask compared with the ground truth.

---

**Q1.** A mask has TP = 80, FP = 20, FN = 40. Compute precision, recall and Dice.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
TN is not needed.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Precision $80/100 = 0.80$, recall $80/120 = 0.67$, Dice $160/(160 + 60) = 0.73$.
:::

---

**Q2.** Why can a useless segmentation have 99 % accuracy?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Think of an image with very few object pixels.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
If objects are 1 % of the pixels, calling everything background gets 99 % of the pixels right (all TN) while finding nothing. Accuracy is dominated by the true negatives.
:::

---

**Q3.** Dice is 0.9. What is the Jaccard index?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$J = D/(2 - D)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$0.9/1.1 = 0.82$. Jaccard is always smaller than Dice (except at 0 and 1), but ranks masks in the same order.
:::

---

**Q4.** Where on the ROC plot are the points for "everything is object" and "nothing is object"?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Compute TPR and FPR in both cases.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Everything object: TPR = 1, FPR = 1, the top-right corner. Nothing object: TPR = 0, FPR = 0, the bottom-left corner. Every threshold lies on the curve between them.
:::

---

**Q5.** A method's ROC curve is the diagonal from $(0, 0)$ to $(1, 1)$. What is its AUC, and what does that say about the grey levels?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
AUC = the probability that an object pixel is brighter than a background pixel.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
AUC = 0.5: an object pixel is brighter than a background pixel only half the time, as by chance. The grey level carries no information about the class.
:::

---

**Q6.** Two methods have the same ROC curve, but you test them on images where objects are 0.5 % of the pixels. Why should you also look at the precision–recall curve?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How many false positives does an FPR of 0.02 mean here?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
FPR is a fraction of the huge background: 2 % of 99.5 % of the pixels is four times the whole object. The ROC point still looks good, but precision is poor. The PR curve shows how many false positives come with each true one.
:::

---

**Q7.** A segmentation merges every pair of touching cells into one blob, otherwise perfectly. Is its Dice high or low? Is it a good segmentation for counting cells?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which pixels are wrong?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Dice is close to 1: almost every pixel has the right label (only the thin boundary between touching cells is wrong). For counting it is bad: every touching pair counts as one cell. Pixel measures do not see objects; object-level evaluation (day 16) does.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Show that Dice is the harmonic mean of precision and recall.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$1/p = (TP + FP)/TP$ and $1/r = (TP + FN)/TP$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\frac{2}{1/p + 1/r} = \frac{2\,TP}{(TP + FP) + (TP + FN)} = \frac{2\,TP}{2\,TP + FP + FN}$, which is Dice.
:::
